> [View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9MURGjjG4aA&lc=UgzbvWbn76lxg2ZeM8p4AaABAg.AOINocCTOIZAOOjK6fSbOb)  
>
> This lecture attempts to explain “the theory of everything” by combining cosmology, evolution, neuroscience, and metaphysics, but it mixes accurate facts with major misconceptions and logical errors. The first issue appears in the description of the Big Bang. The talk treats the Big Bang as a ball of energy exploding into space, when in reality it describes space itself expanding from a hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago. There was no “outside” for it to explode into. The claim that the universe should expand linearly is false general relativity predicts different expansion rates over time, with an early decelerating phase and a later accelerating one. The statement that some parts of the universe expand faster than others misunderstands the difference between uniform cosmic expansion and local gravitational motions. The idea that dark energy is “cheating” also misunderstands science dark energy is an empirical parameter inferred from multiple observations, not a hand wave. Current evidence shows about 68 percent of the cosmic energy density is dark energy, not 80–90 percent. The “multiple Big Bangs” alternative adds speculation without predictive power or data support.  
>   
> The treatment of evolution also misuses facts. Evolution does not “fail” for humans it applies as well to us as to any other species. Humans share about 98–99 percent of DNA with chimpanzees, not 99.9 percent, and small regulatory genetic differences explain large cognitive and behavioral changes. The idea that humans have existed for 200,000 years but only 50,000 years of “history” confuses written history with archaeological evidence, which extends well beyond 50,000 years. Evolution does not predict multiple coexisting human species today extinction of sister lineages such as Neanderthals and Denisovans is normal. The argument that “evolution should produce humans with three eyes or six fingers” misunderstands mutation and developmental constraints evolution works through gradual modification within viable anatomical limits.  
>   
> The discussion of the human mind and memory also includes major errors. Neuroscience has identified where and how memory is stored the hippocampus is crucial for forming new episodic memories, and long term storage is distributed across the neocortex. Saying “we don’t know where memory is stored” ignores a century of converging evidence. Memories are not organized by “emotion folders” such as happy or sad emotions modulate how memories are encoded, but storage is not categorical. Babies can form memories and display temperament long before they form a worldview, so their individuality poses no contradiction. The description of neurons “hitting each other to create electricity” is inaccurate neurons transmit electrochemical signals across synapses in measurable, well understood ways.  
>   
> The section contrasting imagination with the scientific method sets up a false dichotomy. Inspiration often precedes systematic testing, but scientific creativity and the method complement each other. Einstein’s relativity arose from imaginative thought experiments combined with rigorous mathematics and later experimental confirmation. Watson and Crick’s DNA model was built from hard data, not dreams. Claiming that no great idea ever came from the scientific method ignores the iterative process of hypothesis, prediction, and testing that validates imagination and turns it into knowledge.  
>   
> The quantum mechanics explanation is partially correct electrons are field excitations and quantum systems can exist in superpositions but the conclusion that “there is no objective reality” misuses philosophical interpretations. Schrödinger’s cat is a thought experiment about measurement, not literal proof that reality is subjective. Modern quantum theory explains classical definiteness through decoherence, showing how macroscopic objects have stable states without requiring observers to create them.  
>   
> Later sections use near death experiences, psychedelics, and literature as evidence for a spiritual dimension. While such experiences are interesting, they are anecdotal and not scientific proof of a higher realm. Neurobiology offers testable accounts oxygen deprivation and serotonin receptor activity explain many of their reported features. Shared imagery across cultures can arise from common human neurobiology and communication, not necessarily from universal metaphysical truths.  
>   
> The final section turns into a conspiracy narrative claiming that science exists to erase God and that secret societies worship Satan to invert heaven and hell. This mixes category errors and unfalsifiable assertions. Science is a method for testing models, not a belief system about divinity. Claims of global coordination by secret groups controlling scientific knowledge lack evidence and fail basic logical standards such as burden of proof and parsimony. Invoking such conspiracies adds nothing explanatory human behavior, institutional incentives, and normal sociological dynamics already account for how ideas spread.  
>   
> Logically, the lecture commits several recurring fallacies straw man arguments (misstating scientific theories), arguments from ignorance (“we don’t know dark energy, therefore the Big Bang is wrong”), false dichotomies (imagination vs method, spirit vs matter), and non sequiturs (space travel proves heaven is destroyed). The reasoning also moves goalposts, equivocates on “random,” and generalizes from anecdotes to universals. In short, the talk’s imaginative energy is engaging, but its scientific content collapses under factual scrutiny. A coherent presentation should clearly separate established evidence, open scientific questions, philosophical speculation, and personal belief without confusing one for another.

As a biologist, my main gripe with the critique of evolution using the lack of human diversity as an example is that what defines a species is arbitrary. There's more diversity in Homo sapiens than you think.

In practice, the physiological differences that separate different species are often very small: The difference between red vs black oak is the presence of tiny hairs in the crotches of the leaf veins and a different acorn cap. The difference between sugar maple vs black maple is a slightly different leaf shape, with a different number of lobes. The difference between white ash vs green ash is a differently shaped leaf scar, and different colored buds. The difference between prairie voles and meadow voles is that one of them pair bonds and mates for life. Black capped chickadees vs carolina chickadees = different songs. Harbor seals vs spotted seals? Different vocalizations and slightly different spotting pattern.

If humans were any other animal, we'd consider each race a separate subspecies, due to differences in skin pigmentation, hair texture, bone density/structure, lactose intolerance, altitude adaptation, malaria resistance, body build, etc.

As much as I love your videos and will continue to support you, this video reminded me that you are a human being with intelligent opinions.

Not sure much about the neuroscience, but there’s a huge lack of understanding in physics and evolution. 

Furthermore, touting science as a religion and a power grab seems to miss the point that scientific theories aren’t about what’s right, but what’s the least wrong so far.

Also, the examples of Newton and Einstein and to compare it to how a novelist writes is not an accurate parallel. First, those two physicists are in an extreme minority and not what majority of development in physics happens. Majority of physics has been based on countless observations and experiments. Which leads to the second point, which is that Newton and Einstein’s theories were both based on observations and experiments. They were pondering about those experiments and like a lightning strike, understood the underlying principle. Sure, many scientists have ideas first and try to develop an experiment to see if their idea holds. The student’s question was spot on. But majority of the time, it’s wrong. That doesn’t make their pursuit of science less valuable because their idea had led them to experiments that gathered data that may eventually lead to a core realization. Maybe for a future Einstein.

And Wigner’s friend and Schrodinger’s cat are both thought experiments. They don’t have a conclusion similar to how Mary’s room can be argued for both physicalism and idealism. It hasn’t been properly tested, and may never be possible, unless someone like Bell can find an experimental basis to test such a thought experiment (Bell’s Theorem).

I think a core issue with how people who don’t get a real chance to better understand science is that they get fascinated by theoretical/philosophical implications of science, but tend to overlook the theory and the evidence behind it. Conversely, it’s the same for atheists who tout that science is facts. It’s not, it’s just the least wrong. Science is a humble pursuit of observing and understanding what’s around us.

Denying scientific theories because “it doesn’t make sense” without properly demonstrating why their scientific reasoning is the wrong conclusion based on the data is egregious.

Anyways, I love your videos! It reminded me to take your lectures as a spark of inspiration, rather than an esoteric dogma.

>
> Two things can be true at once: the broad science is solid AND specific mechanisms remain genuinely unresolved.  
>   
> Memory: We know the hippocampus is involved in forming memories (Patient H.M. proved this in the 1950s — remove it and you can't form new ones, but old ones survive, so it's clearly not the storage site). We know the amygdala handles fear memory, cerebellum handles motor memory. Nobody disputes this. But the actual question — how does a neuron physically hold a specific memory for 60 years when synaptic proteins turn over every few weeks? — has no confirmed answer. LTP is the best model we have, not a complete explanation. Tonegawa won a Nobel and his engram work still can't explain long-term molecular persistence. If you think this is settled, name the mechanism. Specifically.  
>   
> Human evolution: The fossil lineage from early hominins to Homo sapiens is real and well-supported. Nobody is disputing common descent. The open questions are narrower: (1) What specifically caused the brain to nearly triple in size in roughly 2 million years? Cooking, meat, social complexity, language — all proposed, none confirmed causal. Pick one and try to defend it without the others and you'll see the problem. (2) Most successful mammalian genera have multiple living species — Canis has about 35, Panthera has 5, even Pan has 2. Homo has 1. Neanderthals, Denisovans, Homo erectus, floresiensis all gone. "We outcompeted them" is a narrative, not a mechanism. What specifically gave Sapiens the edge, and why did it result in total extinction rather than niche coexistence, which is the norm in ecology?  
>   
> Calling these questions "cringe" or saying they "gave you cramps" is not a rebuttal. If you have specific answers, share them. That's how science works.Also — leading with "as a biologist" isn't an argument. It's a credential. Credentials tell me you passed exams, not that you have answers to open questions. Tonegawa is a Nobel laureate molecular biologist and he'll tell you memory encoding isn't solved. Eric Kandel won the Nobel for memory research and his work covers Aplysia sea slugs, not human episodic memory persistence. If Nobel winners in the actual subfield are still publishing competing hypotheses, a YouTube commenter saying "as a biologist, this gave me cramps" might want to be a bit more specific about what exactly they know that Tonegawa doesn't.

I absolutely love these videos and find them so eye-opening, but as an evolution believer and having a bio degree I have to share some of my more skeptical thoughts when it comes to Jiang’s understanding of evolution… and I will add before I continue that I was hoping Jiang would be able to change my mind on the subject and show me that science may be hiding something more. But for the reasons, I will explain I am still skeptical. I definitely invite others to share their replies on these thoughts because I’m so curious. 
When it comes to human evolution, scientists believe that the last common grandmother of the chimp and the human would have been about 6 million years ago, and the very first and earliest humans would have evolved 2.5 million years ago. Still quite a lot of time missing there. So I don’t necessarily agree with him saying that scientists don’t know how we went from ape to chimp as they have a fairly confident idea, just not with every single piece of the puzzle. 
Science does indeed say there were at least five other human species on earth. A couple of them lived in remote places, such as the dwarf species of Indonesia.  Homo erectus were the first to use fire and hunting weapons. Neanderthals had the largest brains and were very muscular, and bred with sapiens (us, and the last remaining species). Sapiens evolved in Africa about 300Kyears ago, so they coexisted with Neanderthals and a couple of the other human species on earth until about 30K years ago with the extinction of the Neanderthals.
Perhaps the most mysterious development was the sudden jump to the top of the food chain 100K yrs ago and the spread from Africa 70K yrs ago by Homo sapiens. 
This leads to my next problem with Jiang‘s problems.  When it comes to his point that there should be more species of human and far more diversity, again I disagree and would reply that the small variations among races reflect this idea, however, there has simply not been enough time since the spread from Africa to evolve into much different beings from one another apart from that. For example on Jiang‘s idea that there should be varying human species around the world, to entertain that thought we could expect the people of arctic regions to evolve to have something like fur. The thing about evolution is that it requires time and the pressure to survive.  Because Homo sapiens had certainly started creating clothing and domesticating fire by the time they spread into arctic regions, they did not have this pressure to survive and stay warm by growing fur- they had already adapted in other ways, due to their cognitive abilities. Scientists do find the cognitive revolution fascinating and mysterious, but their explanation from what I’ve read is that our cognitive abilities are a result of the domestication of fire (having cooked food meant we didn’t need huge jaw muscles and had more room to grow brains) and our ability to communicate with one another.
ANYWAY so sorry for this super long comment, but I wanted to share everything that I have read that would contradict what Jiang is presenting here about the origins of early humans. As a fairly science minded person, I tend to have a hard time moving beyond this frame of mind, so I am eager to hear other people’s research as well.

I've been enjoying this series, but Prof Jiang's framing of cosmological expansion is completely wrong.  We see that the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it moves away.  This implies a very smooth and even expansion across the universe, specifically in intergalactic space.  This is not conjecture, that part is observed fact.

The idea of dark energy is to acknowledge that we don't have the ability to observe what is causing that expansion.  The only mechanism we've had for observing objects in space has been light, so we call it dark energy because whatever is causing that expansion isn't giving off light.

This has legitimately impacted my respect for Jiang if he's willing to misrepresent scientific theory and observed facts that badly.

### **@grizzlydoormat** | 👍 41 likes
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9MURGjjG4aA&lc=UgyRDL-x6oX94I-AyfZ4AaABAg)

SCIENCE IS A MIRACLE

Jiang: “PLEASE CHALLENGE ME!”  
Student: “Eh? I don’t think that is right.”
Jiang: “YOU JUST DONT SEE IT. LETS MOVE ON!”

Allow me to help out the confused and neglected students:

I regularly follow Jiang's lectures, and appreciate his fresh take on forces that shape history, particularly about the rise and decline of empires.  I am aware that not all interpretations presented are accurate or correct, but they are models or frameworks to help guide our thinking, and we have to arrive at our own conclusions. However, when it comes to science, there is a rigorous way to evaluate the validity of models or hypothesis before they are accepted as established theories.  In this particular lecture, which focused more on scientific topics than historical ones, there are large gaps in Jiang's understanding of the scientific method and the three areas he discussed: cosmology, the origin and evolution of life, and neural science.  And he left the impression that scientific theories are up for individual interpretations driven by intuition.  There are rooms for alternative interpretation of objective data in science, but the wiggle room is small.  And the standard is higher for these interpretations to become established theories than in other disciplines such as history.

Still, I appreciate that his alternative hypotheses are suitable for high school students and offer a refreshing perspective in their liberal arts education. While simplifying concepts can mean sacrificing accuracy, as Jiang has noted, it's sometimes necessary. However, correcting some fundamental inaccuracies is important for general audiences.  As it will shape peoples perception of science and scientific process. I will simply point out a few noticeable errors:


1)	Jiang largely reflected the public's misconception regarding "Dark Energy." Contrary to the claim that it is widely accepted, Dark Energy remains a provisional concept within the scientific community. Researchers continue to seek more comprehensive explanations or deeper understanding of its nature. Rather than representing any form of deception, Dark Energy currently serves as a placeholder in cosmological models to account for observed phenomena, given the absence of superior alternatives. The broader framework of the big bang theory and cosmology remains highly effective in explaining empirical data, and, for practical purposes, current models provide reliable predictions.


2)	Regarding evolution, Jiang essentially presented a version of teleology as alternative to Darwin's evolution which is based on a process of random mutation and natural selection.   Teleology and many of its variants have been contradicted by current evidence. While some may find it appealing to consider that life and consciousness do not arise solely from random processes, research has shown that Teleology has not been supported by data. Evolutionary theory, similar to cosmology, is not yet complete and there remain unanswered questions (though these are not the ones cited by Jiang). Nevertheless, evolution remains the most comprehensive scientific theory for explaining the available objective data and enables predictions that can be tested in the laboratory. Scientists continue to refine and develop the theory.


3)	Jiang's understanding of neural science is inaccurate. The field lacks a definitive theory of consciousness and historically avoided the topic due to concerns over testability. It is Psychologists who have attempted to develop theories of consciousness, though psychology is not strictly considered a science. Advances in brain imaging bring neuroscience closer to breakthroughs, but a final theory has yet to emerge, as the discipline remains in its early stages.


4)	Jiang incorrectly applied quantum mechanics, which only describes the ultra-microscopic world. His student pointed this out.  "Vibration" in quantum physics is a mathematical concept, distinct from how we use the term in everyday language; physicists borrow these terms just for ease of communication.  The accurate descriptions are in the equations and peer-reviewed scientific papers.


These minor issues are acceptable as "over-simplification for clarity" since he is presenting a powerful idea, not a science lesson.  The mistake below is more serious:



5)	The main mistake in Jiang's presentation concerns the Scientific Method, which actually describes how the scientific community operates rather than individual scientists. This again was called out by his student.  While breakthroughs often stem from personal inspiration and individuals have biases and selfish incentives, the community adheres to rigorous cycles of hypothesis, experimentation, and falsification. For example, Einstein’s Quantum Theory of Light won the Nobel Prize for its ability to explain data, whereas String Theory has not because it remains untested despite the mathematical elegance that appeals to many scientists aesthetics. Authoritarian regimes often oppose science because it challenges unverified claims. Although Jiang suggests higher meaning and religious beliefs are important, science doesn't undermine spirituality—it seeks understanding with careful methodology, serving as a safeguard against ideology.

In conclusion, scientific process and scientific community as a whole institutionalized objective evidence and rigorous testing as bases for establishing theory, precisely because individual scientists are driven by personal inspiration and carry biases.  Although individual scientists may very well "cheat", the scientific enterprise as a whole largely do not.  Public understanding of science may be manipulated, but the scientific community as a whole has upheld its integrity.  There are many historical precedents where authoritarian regimes try to coopt the scientific community but science ultimately prevailed.  And that is the message that Jiang did not get right.

### **@Cybernaut77** | 👍 65 likes

As a physics student, I think you misunderstand modern cosmology, the big bang model and dark energy.
First of all, the big isn't supposed to be a localised event, but rather something that happened everywhere in the universe at once, it was the start of the universe's expansion
Second of all, the expansion of the universe does not vary randomly between different regions like you claim, it is consistent and mostly linear, it has changed with time, however, and that's where dark energy or the cosmological constant comes in. General relativity predicts that in a universe with only matter and radiation, the total self-gravitation of it all should slow the expansion of the universe down, eventually reverse it and cause a re-collapse, a big crunch. However physicists later discovered that, instead of slowing down, the expansion of the universe is accelerating. So they amended the original equations with an additional term - the cosmological constant - that represents this unknown force accelerating the universe's expansion, which is nowadays known as dark energy. It is indeed unknown to us so far what exactly it is, but I wouldn't call it lazy, it's more of a placeholder for when/if we ever discover what it really is. 

Interestingly, recent universe surveys with modern telescopes is actually starting to challenge this idea though, mainly because there's some tentative evidence that dark energy is not a constant, but rather might be evolving with time, potentially weakening.

Srinivasa Ramanujan can be considered an example of the scientific method working in reverse. He produced many mathematical formulas, identities, and theorems without initially providing formal proofs. Remarkably, many of these results were later verified by other mathematicians using rigorous mathematical methods, while some are still being studied and proved today. Ramanujan himself believed that the goddess Namagiri appeared in his dreams and revealed mathematical insights to him, which he then recorded in his notebooks. Despite having little formal training in advanced mathematics, his intuition was extraordinary. Tragically, he died at the young age of 32, yet in that short time he made profound contributions to mathematics that continue to influence the field today.

Einstein developed a system of taking naps with steel balls in his hands and a steel bowl at his feet, and between his brain falling asleep and reassembling and building connections of what he was learning/grappling with at the time, he exploited this moment of the brain to come up with many things. 
Jiang is precisely the kind of person educated on enough things to come up with interconnected ideas and teach in a gestalt manner, but still feels pressed to explain it all using divinity. ### **@amankota19** | 👍 2 likes
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9MURGjjG4aA&lc=Ugx958YKHFjFmMBe2Yx4AaABAg)

wait, it started off really good. But then📉 when you mentioned the 'spirit world.' (I’d need more explanation on why you think that exists). Instead, I think the process is more grounded.

Take Ramanujan, for example. Equations used to pop into his head like random cravings for normal people. On his deathbed, he told Hardy that the Hindu goddess of knowledge showed him these equations in dreams. He even said, 'An equation means nothing to me unless it expresses a thought of God.' What is fascinating is that these weren't just random visions, they were concrete, fully functioning equations that he would later verify and derive. 

Consider Ramanujan’s equations from over a century ago. Long before the discovery of black holes, he wrote mock theta functions that today describe black hole characteristics better than almost anything else. Guess what's even more interesting: he didn't even know what a black hole was to begin with.

This implies that the context of the problem wasn't required for his subconscious to solve it. But , the format of the answer was dictated by his environment. Born into a Brahmin family, his brain developed in an atmosphere steeped in divinity. His neural pathways were strongly wired with a dual obsession: God and Mathematics + some other tiny variables.

Just imagine the absurdity of it: a tiny, biological speck in the grand scheme of the cosmos, residing on a rock trillions of miles away, creating a measuring device for something he has never seen, heard, or held. t’s like eating a fruit that only you have tasted, and trying to explain the flavor to a friend using only words. For someone like him, it isn't a cliché to say his brain spoke the language of mathematics. While we have an internal monologue in English or our native tongue, his internal narrative was likely composed of numbers and patterns. He didn't just 'do' math; he perceived nature as math. He lived for math, he breathes maths and died for maths. With clear, sole mind for maths and his environment falicitated for him to become something beyond common comprehension.
.
His obsession was so intense that he would forget to eat while working. This confirms that the conscious mind drives the unconscious. Because his conscious mind believed deeply in God, his unconscious mind delivered the ideas in that specific format. Think of it like a computer file: the raw data (the math) is the same, but his brain could only open it in 'MP3 format' (divine vision) because that was the software he had installed.

Therefore, it isn't necessarily a 'Divine Force.' When inexplicable things happen, humans tend to stop investigating and just slap a label on it, like you mentioned  'Dark Matter' or  'Good Luck/bad luck by common people when they don't understand why did this happen and they start doing rituals.  But if you dissect Ramanujan's case, you see the mechanism: to keep his reality intact, he needed to receive those equations from God.

Basically, if your obsession to find an answer is enduranced enough (not soemthing for tiny amount of time but for long time), you will get it. But first, the mind must be cleared to focus solely on that one thing without distraction. This is exactly how ancient Gurus achieved enlightenment; Ramanujan was simply 'enlightened' in the field of mathematics. You create energy by focusing, redirecting the massive power of the unconscious mind through a single conscious thought.

If we want answers, unravelling the human mind is the most important step. We try to justify the grand cosmos based on our limited experience, but ultimately, we are viewing the universe through the lens of our own culture and mental wiring.
As you mentioned, for every great thinker, ideas seem to turn on suddenly like a lightbulb. I don't have enough evidence to say this comes from a higher being. Based on looking within myself and tracking how ideas form, I believe it’s the unconscious mind grinding away like a pot of food slowly cooking in the background.

You stick with a problem and tell the 'Magic Box' (your subconscious) that this is what you need. The Magic Box starts working on the answer from that moment, though it diminishes if your will to find the answer is weak. It tailors all your past experiences to lead to a solution, and one day, it spits out an idea that looks random and sudden. The conscious mind then processes it, and voila-  you have the idea.

The Magic Box is essentially an algorithm processing a huge number of possibilities that we don't consciously experience. To process those possibilities, one needs the data, the data is nothing but all the exp + environment + knowledge + emotion and all those minute details that we tend to ignore builds up something amazin of an idea. The 'Divine Force' might just be the communication loop between the environment, our consciousness (knowlege, understadning, ego, everything that makes up) , and our unconscious mind. We are simply trapped in this loop, perhaps we need something new somethng otherworldly to free us from this loop ( This is how a religion was born in lower level of thinking).

That’s why I’ve always wondered: if aliens came from intergalactic space, I would want to communicate with them. cause something is completely new, something which beyond the new, they might be able to see what we may not or show us the right software to intall in our brain. They might show us or make us realize it’s all just a game of the mind, and that we are trapped between our environment and our conscious/unconscious processing. We again fall in the loop, do we really have a free will? I say no but we do have certain free will up to certain extent. We increase our free will by climbing the floors like a level to conqure until then we have very less percentage of free will. Every action is influnced by our mind. All these are just surface level, I am afraid the coment section might not be enough to write it down.

### **@KevinDeSimone-y8j** | 👍 1 likes
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9MURGjjG4aA&lc=UgyudF8Djw4wKoW_9J14AaABAg)

Professor, you're right that neuroscience hasn't figured out "where" memories are stored, if your model of memory storage is like a mailroom with discrete events in time being slotted into a discrete physiological substrate. Lashley showed that you can't resect the brain to destroy memories. This is foundational neuroscience, and that conundrum was a lesson in my neuroscience education. Let's not pretend that neuroscientists don't understand this complexity.

Your student asked about the hippocampus, and your answer wasn't bad. But the right answer to their question is that the hippocampus consolidates memories, meaning it's crucially important for transitioning working memory to long term memory (not that the hippocampus itself stores memories, which are also referred to as engrams, see Lashley again). The studies of brain damaged patients like HM have provided pretty conclusive evidence about the role of hippocampus in memory consolidation, but they haven't resulted in knowing "where" a memory exists in the neural substrate. It isn't as simple as this, as you say.

But your question remains: once a long-term memory has formed (ie an experience transitions from short-term to long-term storage), where is this represented in the brain physiologically?  The best neuroscientific answer I've come by is that when we recollect a past event, it appears as if our brain recreates the pattern of activation (albeit dampened, akin to your visual cortex processing light stimuli while under anesthesia) that is observed during the experience itself.  Take a look at Ken Norman and Sean Polyn for the primary evidence, published in Nature and Science. That's profound, and doesn't undermine your thesis here imo.

Happy to talk more about these topics.

- Quantum coherence: A system can exist in a superposition of states (like Schrödinger’s cat being both alive and dead).

- Decoherence: When the system interacts with its environment (photons, air molecules, detectors), information about its state “leaks out.” This entanglement makes interference patterns vanish, and the system appears to settle into one classical outcome.

- Result: The quantum system no longer shows quantum interference; instead, it looks like a classical object with definite properties

14:50 hm by my understanding, and this is basically just my working theory, is that memories are stored in the whole brain. When you have an experience, it causes neurons in the brain to fire. When neurons fire at the same time, they build connections with each other (neurons that fire together wire together). When someone remembers a smell in an mri, the part of their brain where smells are processed lights up. So, the way i see it, experiences are stored in the network of neurons that were firing when you had the experience. And neurons can be part of many many networks, so when you think of a memory you are causing that specific network of neurons to fire, if that makes sense?

Dear Prof Jiang, I have been watching all your lectures so far, and this one is confusing to me. Please I hope you can guide me here.
1. Is Earth the only place where life exists? If God or "The One" wants imagination and growth, wouldn't there be other places with other beings through which imagination can thrive so the universe can expand? 
2. Does this mean there are multiple planets or worlds like Earth where it is exactly the same as here?
3. Since Mars or any other planet is part of our universe, if and when Humans go there, multiply and do the same crap we do here, wouldn't Mars also rebel if there is too much dissonance? Say with Sand Storms and lightning or whatever to remove the dissonance and restore a state of balance?

From here, are some of my thoughts I would love to share with you. Hopefully you find the time.
1. I would encourage you to explore and read about the ritual of "Sandhyavandhanam" done by the Hindu Brahmins in India. It is said that this ritual has the power to purify everything within and around us and create an ambience of positivity. This is not really religion because there is no "belief", but a ritual where there are mantras which help create resonance with energies as you describe. Each mantra invokes a deity who is said to the ruler of an energy type. I say this because I feel you may draw a lot of parallels with the knowledge you possess.
2. There is also a concept of Yuga in Hindu culture - where it depicts the behaviour of society in a cyclical fashion. At the end of the cycle of yuga, the universe is destroyed and is born again. In my culture, the growth of arrogance, pride, ego, selfishness, disrespect and so on, are considered the symptoms of negative energy taking over the person and we have many examples of this.
3. There are various schools of thought of the structure of the universe and the true nature of reality. Two of the most common ones are Advaita Vedanta and Vedanta - these of course predate Greek philosophers, but I find so many parallels. There is a book called Vishwadarshan by Mahatma Ramratna Thapaliyal who explains in extreme detail how the universe is created and what it contains. He says he received this wisdom during his 17-year penance. I hope this gives you fresh perspective. The book talks about how the world is created by the supreme consciousness and Prakriti. How it is maintained and how it is destroyed.

I shared the above because you have way more interconnected lines between knowledge you have gained over time, and hopefully these can lead to new imagination and perspective.

Thank you so much for uploading your lectures to Youtube. I'm so lucky to have discovered you.

### **@LeggoMyEggHo_**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9MURGjjG4aA&lc=Ugz5jDgZKHaxh4QZfeF4AaABAg)

This is exactly why a gene-centered view is incomplete. Sometimes the big change isn’t the gene itself, but the regulatory DNA controlling when and where it’s expressed. Voles are the classic example. Prairie voles are monogamous, while meadow voles are solitary/polygamous. Scientists finally narrowed this down in voles to the differences around Avpr1a shift receptor expression in the brain. To test that hypothesis, they took voles from their habitat and swapped the receptor expression to see if the voles would swap pair-bonding preferences. And it worked.  Same basic toolkit, different regulation, radically different outcome.

In simple terms, the genes are essentially coded storage shelves, meaning changes are sort of isolated. But what about the door, or gate, that can restrict or prevent access to that storage shelf? What if all these storage shelves had their own door, plus a group door that controlled access into all of the doors? What if we grouped storage shelves based on functions, increasing efficiency of the doors (gates)?

Complexity can easily emerge out of simplicity as long as the relational levers between those simple things exist.

Your description of the lecture as a "soup of everything" is accurate. The lecturer is engaging in syncretism—blending unrelated systems (Quantum Physics, German Idealism, and Christian Theology) to create a single narrative.

Here is the breakdown of the "logic" he uses to jump from one disparate idea to the next, and how he attempts to patch the holes you noticed.

1. The Starting Point: Quantum Mechanics as "The Breaker"
He uses Quantum Mechanics not as a scientific model, but as a philosophical weapon to destroy "Materialism."


The Leap: He claims that because atoms are "vibrations" or "probability clouds" rather than solid balls, physical matter does not truly exist.

The Conclusion: If matter isn't solid, then reality must be "mental" or "projected." This clears the table for him to introduce philosophy.

2. The Bridge: Kant and Hegel as "The Fixers"
Once he removes physical matter, he needs a new rulebook for reality. He cherry-picks Kant and Hegel to provide it.


Kant (The Mechanism): He uses Kant to argue that humans "hallucinate" reality using internal filters (Time and Space). This validates his claim that the world is in our heads.

The Problem You Noticed (Qualia/Solipsism): He explicitly raises the problem you mentioned: If we all hallucinate reality, why do we all see the same table? Why isn't it different for everyone? .

Hegel (The Patch): To fix this, he uses Hegel’s concept of Geist (Spirit). He argues we all see the same reality because we are all connected to a single "Central Server" or "Universal Mind". In his view, we are individual screens displaying a signal from the same broadcast.

3. The Religious Layer: The "Monad" becomes "God"
This is the final blend. He takes this "Universal Mind/Monad" and overlays a Christian moral framework onto it.

The Redefinition:

God is the "Monad" or the interconnectivity of the universe.

Satan is not necessarily a guy with a pitchfork, but the concept of Materialism.

The Argument: He argues that "Hell" is the belief that the material world is real, random, and meaningless. If you believe in the Big Bang and "survival of the fittest," you are disconnected from the "Server" (God) and living in fear/isolation (Hell).

The War: The "War between God and Satan" is actually an intellectual war between Idealism (The world is spirit/meaning) and Materialism (The world is matter/randomness).

Summary of the "Soup"
The lecturer is essentially retelling ancient Gnosticism (the idea that the physical world is a trap/illusion and we must wake up to our spiritual nature) but wearing the "costume" of modern science to make it sound authoritative.

He says Quantum Mechanics proves the world is an illusion.

He says DNA/Biology proves we are "avatars."

He says Philosophy proves there is a "Programmer."

He says Theology explains the moral stakes of the simulation.

It is a "soup" because he treats metaphorical similarities as literal proofs, using Hegel to solve a physics problem and Jesus to solve a philosophical one.

### **@CourageFreedom-yo3ul** | 👍 1 likes
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9MURGjjG4aA&lc=Ugwizr6cj6gcvWfZ40l4AaABAg)

Some of the misrepresentation in this video maybe due to the instructor’s personal experience, or perhaps intentionally using a straw man argument to create a stronger “wow” factor in his academic presentation.
As a long-time tutor and private instructor in the U.S., I can say that I have never seen modern scientific literature present the scientific method as a strictly linear approach, as he describes. In fact, the dozens of sources I’ve reviewed over the years consistently emphasize that the scientific method is not linear and often begins with an idea.
Starting from a “brilliant” idea can also be problematic and may not always lead to great discoveries. For example, a pharmaceutical company might hire a team of scientists and direct them to begin with the assumption that a certain drug cures a particular ailment—then develop a process intended to prove just that. Is that a good thing?
Sometimes a linear approach is useful, and other times it isn’t. Maybe I just had good teachers—or was a good teacher to myself 🤷🏻‍♀️—but I never grew up thinking the scientific method was linear. The main purpose of studying its components is to highlight the importance of testing explanations against evidence, practicing transparency, and ensuring repeatability—all of which help reduce bias and make results more reliable.
When I taught an astronomy class, I explained what the Big Bang theory was, but not as fact. Afterward, I asked students to raise their hands if they believed the Big Bang theory explained how the universe was created—and not one person raised their hand. Regarding evolution, there is also a group of scientists who developed the theory of intelligent design and heavily critique Charles Darwin.
What the instructor seems to miss is that, at least in the U.S., there exists a wide range of creativity, opinions, philosophies, and ways of thinking. If you are passionate about something, you can find your community and build something meaningful. It feels as though he has had a particular experience or narrow slice of Western culture and assumes it represents everyone’s. It doesn’t. There are so many great thinkers, professors, and institutions out there—seek and you shall find. His lectures are interesting, but presented through a limited lens of experience.

### **@woland27**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9MURGjjG4aA&lc=UgzydACQSekSBxJr97t4AaABAg)

The Argument for Scientific Realism
The lecturer’s "Theory of Everything" is not a theory at all, but a classic "God of the Gaps" fallacy. The entire argument rests on a single, fragile premise: “Because science cannot currently explain X perfectly, my specific spiritual magic Y must be true.”

Here is the systematic invalidation of his points:

1. The "Straw Man" of Broken Science
The lecturer claims scientific models (Big Bang, Evolution) are "broken" because they contain variables we don't yet understand (like Dark Energy). This is a fundamental misunderstanding of how science works.

Correction: Science is iterative. "Dark Energy" isn't a "cheat code" invented to save a broken theory; it is a placeholder label for an observed phenomenon (expansion). Identifying what we don't know is the strength of science, not its death knell.

The Flaw: He demands that science provide absolute, finished truth now. When it honestly reports "we are still investigating this part," he declares the whole system invalid and replaces it with a "magic monad" that explains nothing but "feels" complete.

2. The Quantum Category Error
The lecturer’s pivotal move is equating Quantum Decoherence (a subatomic particle interacting with a field) with Human Conscious Observation (a person looking at a chair).

The Physics:  In quantum mechanics, an "observer" is simply any system (like a photon or a wall) that interacts with a particle. It does not require a conscious human mind. The moon continues to exist even when no one looks at it because it is constantly "observed" by the photons from the sun.

The Counter: We do not "hallucinate" reality. If reality were a subjective hallucination, we could hallucinate ourselves flying or walking through walls. The fact that we essentially cannot violate the laws of physics with our minds proves that the material world exists independently of our wishes.

3. The "Radio Receiver" Fallacy (Neuroscience)
He argues the brain doesn't generate consciousness but "receives" it like a radio tuning into a signal (the Monad).

The Rebuttal: If the brain were just a receiver, damaging it would only distort the signal (like a fuzzy radio), but the "music" (the personality/soul) should remain intact.

The Evidence: Neuroscience shows that physical damage to specific brain areas can fundamentally change who you are—erasing memories, changing your personality, or removing your ability to feel fear (e.g., Phineas Gage). If the "soul" were a remote signal, brain damage shouldn't be able to rewrite your personality. This proves the mind is inextricably tied to the wetware of the brain.

4. The "Cosmic Serpent" is Pareidolia
The claim that ancient snake art proves knowledge of DNA is a textbook example of Pareidolia—the brain's tendency to find meaningful patterns in random noise.

Evolutionary Reality:

Humans evolved in environments where snakes were a primary predator. We are hardwired to notice and mythologize snake shapes (winding, spiral forms). Seeing a "double helix" in a drawing of two snakes intertwining is coincidence, not microscopy.

The Counter: If ancients had access to molecular biology via visions, why did they only "see" the shape of DNA? Why didn't they give us the cure for smallpox, the structure of the atom, or the germ theory of disease? They only "knew" things that fit vague artistic patterns, which suggests they didn't actually know them at all.

Final Verdict: The "Comfort Trap"
The lecturer's argument is emotionally satisfying but logically hollow. He creates a false dichotomy: "Either Science explains everything perfectly right now, or you are an avatar in a spiritual war."

The reality is much simpler: We are evolved primates on a rock in a vast, indifferent universe, slowly learning how it works through trial and error. The lecturer’s "Theory" is a defense mechanism—a way to pretend we are the center of the universe (Avatars of a God) so we don't have to face the vast, quiet reality that science reveals.
